review: Finally 100% the game nine years after I firt played it. An unforgettable game with tons of charm, the music is a special highlight for me too.

Forget Me Not: My Organic Garden is one of the most unusual indie simulation games ever created, blending farming mechanics, clicker-style progression, visual novel storytelling, and surreal body horror into an experience that feels strangely comforting and deeply unsettling at the same time. What initially appears to be a quirky management game about growing organs inside a greenhouse slowly transforms into something far more atmospheric and emotionally layered. Beneath the repetitive farming mechanics and soft visual style lies a surprisingly haunting story about identity, routine, and the disturbing normalization of impossible things.

The premise alone immediately makes the game stand out. Players take control of Organa, a young apprentice working for a woman named Irene in a peaceful village shop that specializes in cultivating human organs like crops. Hearts, lungs, kidneys, and other body parts are planted, watered, harvested, and sold to customers as though they were ordinary vegetables. The world treats this bizarre process as completely normal, and that calm acceptance of something grotesque creates the game’s uniquely surreal atmosphere. Instead of relying on graphic horror, the game becomes unsettling through its quiet normality and dreamlike presentation.

The gameplay revolves primarily around growing and harvesting organs while fulfilling requests from customers visiting the shop. Players repeatedly water organ plants, monitor their growth, collect them at the proper quality level, and complete delivery orders in exchange for money and progression. At first the mechanics feel extremely simple, almost resembling a basic idle or clicker game, but the loop gradually becomes surprisingly addictive as more organ types, upgrades, and management systems unlock. The constant cycle of planting, harvesting, and fulfilling requests creates a strangely hypnotic rhythm that becomes central to the game’s atmosphere.

One of the most interesting aspects of the experience is how repetition itself becomes part of the storytelling. The routine of growing organs eventually starts to feel natural despite the disturbing premise, mirroring how Organa adapts to life inside Irene’s greenhouse. The game intentionally blurs the line between comfort and discomfort, encouraging players to settle into an unsettling daily routine while quietly hinting that something deeply wrong exists beneath the surface of the village. That emotional contradiction gives the game much of its identity.

Progression systems help maintain engagement throughout the experience. Completing customer requests unlocks additional organ types, greenhouse expansions, better tools, and efficiency upgrades that gradually transform the simple farming loop into a more involved management system. The satisfaction of optimizing organ production and building a more efficient greenhouse creates a rewarding sense of advancement even though the core gameplay remains relatively straightforward.

The narrative unfolds slowly through conversations with customers and interactions between Organa and Irene. At first, the story feels almost slice-of-life in tone, focusing on everyday tasks and the strange routines of the village. However, darker themes gradually emerge involving obsession, sacrifice, memory, and the disturbing nature of the world itself. The game avoids directly explaining everything immediately, instead allowing atmosphere, implication, and subtle storytelling to create tension and mystery over time. This slower approach makes later revelations significantly more impactful.

The characters contribute heavily to the game’s charm and emotional weight. Customers arriving at the shop range from eccentric and humorous to quietly disturbing, each bringing their own strange requests and stories into the narrative. Irene is especially memorable because of how calm and affectionate she appears despite the grotesque work surrounding her. Her relationship with Organa develops gradually and becomes one of the emotional foundations of the story, adding warmth to a world that constantly feels slightly wrong.

Visually, the game uses a soft cartoon-inspired art style that contrasts sharply against the disturbing premise. The organs themselves are colorful and oddly cute rather than graphic or horrifying, allowing the game to maintain a strange dreamlike quality throughout the experience. Character portraits are expressive, environments are warm and inviting, and the overall presentation feels intentionally cozy despite the body-horror themes hidden beneath the surface. This contrast between comforting visuals and unsettling concepts is one of the game’s greatest strengths.

The soundtrack also deserves considerable praise. Gentle melodies, music-box themes, and melancholic ambient tracks constantly shift between peaceful and eerie, perfectly supporting the emotional tone of the story. The music rarely becomes loud or dramatic, instead quietly reinforcing the unsettling atmosphere and emotional melancholy surrounding the greenhouse and its inhabitants. Combined with the repetitive farming mechanics, the soundtrack helps create an experience that feels strangely meditative.

However, the game is not without flaws. The repetitive nature of the gameplay can eventually become exhausting, especially during later stages where progression requires large quantities of specific organs and extensive grinding. Players who dislike clicker-style mechanics may struggle with how heavily the experience depends on repetitive harvesting loops and resource management.

The interface also becomes somewhat cluttered as more organ types and systems unlock. Managing the greenhouse efficiently during later stages can feel tedious, and certain mechanics are not explained clearly enough for new players. Some progression requirements become confusing without experimentation or outside guidance, which may frustrate players looking for a smoother management experience.

Pacing can also become uneven. While the slower progression contributes heavily to the game’s atmosphere, certain sections drag due to repetitive grinding and limited gameplay variety. The strongest elements of the experience are clearly its atmosphere and storytelling rather than the complexity of its mechanics.

Despite these weaknesses, Forget Me Not: My Organic Garden succeeds because of how confidently it embraces its bizarre concept. Very few games attempt to combine cozy farming gameplay with surreal body horror and emotional storytelling so naturally. The game constantly feels strange and uncomfortable, yet also oddly relaxing and emotionally sincere at the same time.

What ultimately makes the experience memorable is the emotional contradiction at its core. The game somehow turns the repetitive act of harvesting human organs into something peaceful while gradually revealing darker truths hiding beneath its comforting surface. That balance between warmth and unease gives the game a personality unlike almost anything else in the indie simulation genre.

Forget Me Not: My Organic Garden is not a game designed for everyone. Its repetitive structure, slower pacing, and unsettling themes will likely alienate some players. However, those willing to embrace its strange atmosphere and surreal storytelling will discover one of the most original and emotionally distinctive indie management games available. Its combination of farming mechanics, atmospheric storytelling, memorable music, and bizarre world-building creates an experience that lingers long after the final harvest.

While I recommend this game overall, I must say right off the bat that I would NOT recommend if you: don't like slow progression, don't like hours of grinding, or playing games where you repeat simple gameplay loops as you listen to a show/podcast/music/etc.

Still with me? OK, let's get into why you should play it.
Cavyhouse likes thinking outside of the box. The overall atmosphere of Forget Me Not is both charmingly relaxing with a steady reminder that the premise, as well as the stories you encounter, are a bit morbid. It doesn't venture into horror, but frequently reminds us about the fragility of life. I won't spoil the details, but each and every visitor has their own unique tale to tell, and I was intrigued by them all. The music and sound design of this game is also impeccable; for the long hours you'll be listening to the garden's song, you'll feel very relaxed. And funny enough, the quest noises are incredibly pleasing.
 
I recommend setting up an autoclicker for the early to midgame, because you only get garden-wide tools at endgame. You will have to switch the clicker on and off a lot though, because you will need a lot of single inputs in between. For example, instead of constantly having to hold down LMB to water, I let the clicker do it for me, but I would have to switch it off to put the watering can back or else the game would think I was repeatedly picking it up and down. It's up to you, but it personally saved my right hand from things like the literal hundreds of harvesting clicks until you get the shears, which only happens after you finish the base story, and it really adds up over time.

The grind isn't for everyone, and that is totally OK! But I know some people out there are like me and enjoy completing quests, the steady rise in numbers, and finally hearing that satisfying ping after doing something over and over. If that sort of thing tickles your brain, you will love it. The 'true ending' is what some would say is a rather small scene, but in my opinion, wraps the story up in a cute little bow, and I enjoyed earning it. 

If you don't mind spending a whole day relaxing inside a cute little organ garden, then I would definitely recommend Forget Me Not to you.

This is the only clicker game I think I've ever played, and it is entirely due to the unique concept and art drawing me in. For those unfamiliar, a clicker game is a type of game with minimal explicit gameplay outside of clicking an element or set of elements in the game to advance it. 

Clicker games are often extremely simple and in the worst cases find ways to layer in microtransactions to exploit people, but Forget Me Not is unique in that it's a tiny bit more complicated and doesn't seek to charge you for silly nonsense like energy to keep clicking or whatever. However, while it is a little more complicated, it's still a clicker game, so the gameplay still amounts to repetitive clicking which can grow very tedious and annoying if you're really just wanting to see the story move along.

Normally, I can't stand games with such blatantly repetitive, tedious gameplay, but there is something about how Forget Me Not does it that for some reason makes this...Less annoying to me. I think it's helped more by how it's folded into the narrative, as you're the apprentice of the shop owner and so of course you're doing much of the busywork of tending the shop garden. You're not some hero that finds themselves roped into a bunch of townspeople's chores and have to run out into the wilderness or across town and back to the townsperson for some experience and reward...You're just a shopkeep's apprentice.

That said, it is still a game I can only stand to play occasionally as a result of its simplicity & repetition, and what draws me back is my curiosity about the story and enjoying the artwork. If the art & story don't really catch your interest, then you may well want to skip this. [i]However,[/i] they do have a more involved, albeit still simple, dungeon crawling game where you play as Irene called [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/1396980/The_Sealed_Ampoule]The Sealed Ampoule[/url] that you might enjoy more. It's set prior to this game, so you don't need to have played this one to get into it, and I've found it pretty enjoyable!

On one hand, this game genre and gameplay(clicker game with no automation) make it a hard sell. On the other, I'm confident in saying there is nothing else quite like this game, and it nails it particular aesthetic both stylistically and mechanically. That alone makes this a worthwhile game to play, but only if you have the endurance to 100% complete the game.

If you get the game, you'll probably need to get full completion to feel satisfied with the story. This is hard because the gameplay past the first ending is virtually designed to wear on your patience. There is a post in the community hub that shows the true ending, but I would suggest playing through it because the slog is an in universe part of the story. With that in mind, here are some tips that make the end game go faster.
*Once you have the zoo achievement, release all your butterflies immediately
-Releasing other animals reduces lag, I didn't run into lag issues, but some animals do become useless after a certain point
*Focus on the Linguals first. You'll know it when you see it
*Pickled organs go for slightly more than their excellent counterparts
*Use all the above information to farm for colon tree sap to make those last few quest faster by doing them all at once

If you can dedicate yourself to all that I'm sure it will be a worthwhile experience!

You know those frequently-memed Steam reviews that say Not Recommended, but have ridiculously long playtimes? This game is probably the closest I’m ever going to get to that, because I don’t think you should buy it, but have been inexplicably playing it for long periods of time. I chalk it up to my addiction to collect-a-thons and achievements, because this game has many of those, but it’s kinda just not an objectively good game.

The gameplay is like… just barely gameplay. It’s advertised as something of a gardening sim, but it’s more of a glorified clicker game. You have very little interaction beyond “click on this plant to water it,” “click on this fruit to pick it,” over and over again about a zillion times. The garden art isn’t even that good – in some cases it resembles slightly stylized clipart. And that garden is where you will be spending 80-90% of your playthrough, since there’s no real indication most of the time which quests you finish will trigger new story/character events.

Speaking of that, bad gameplay holds a game back, but sometimes a really good story will make it worthwhile. For example, a fair number of the minigames in the Danganronpa series are objectively bad, but the case storylines and compelling, lovable characters mean that I highly recommend it. Forget Me Not’s character art was so cute and colorful that I looked forward to seeing its story make up for the gameplay, and it… doesn’t at all. I wasn’t attached to a single character, as almost everyone was extremely forgettable, and a significant number of the characters were just plain unlikable (the little girl who [spoiler] *murders her cat* [/spoiler] and says she doesn’t care that [spoiler] her cat’s original soul is dead [/spoiler] as long as she can talk to it, the guy who is so down bad for the blatantly uninterested shopkeeper that he [spoiler] *tries to cut himself open and put organs he purchased from her in his own body to make her love him?? Somehow??* [/spoiler], and even the shopkeeper herself, given that interactions with the farmer reveal [spoiler] she is most likely deliberately destroying his farm and nature in general by having her clueless assistant buy all the animals from that area in order to make him come to her shop and buy things from her [/spoiler]). The protagonist seems to have one singular brain cell. The villain’s motives and backstory are confusing and mostly unexplained. Most of all, you don’t learn enough about any of the characters to really feel for them. And to reach the true ending, which is A. apparently very short, B. could not possibly resolve all the other issues with this story, and C. rather predictable, I suspect, you have to do an ENORMOUS number of fruit harvesting tasks with little to no story events in between. The reason I only *suspect* the true ending is rather predictable is because I haven’t gotten it due to how absurdly long it takes to harvest enough fruits to get it. It’s to the point that one of the game guides says it might not be worth it to do all the tasks and to just look up the true ending yourself. (If I do get there myself, I’ll add that to my review at a later date.)

(More of a minor nitpick, but some of the sound design seems like a strange choice. You have to collect a massive amount of animals to get an achievement, yet every single one of these animals makes noise on a frequent basis. This means that when you have thirty of each animal, it is an auditory nightmare. It’s completely jarring against the calming music of the garden (which is just the same track forever by the way), and sometimes I’d have to take my headphones entirely off so as not to be driven insane. On top of this, the music for the save menu is very clearly London no Shi, which while not an original song (it’s one of those Japanese royalty-free ones), is rather well-known for being used in Misao. If you’re familiar with Misao, then you know it’s a horror game, and London no Shi (which may mean something along the lines of “London’s Death” depending on what kanji is used for “shi”) is one of those songs that sounds like a creepy music box. Why was this chosen for the save menu of a game that's really not very creepy at all? Why was such a distinct track put over only the save menu, which you never remain on for more than a second or two?

Overall, it just feels like wasted potential. A world where organs grow on trees seems like an opportunity to create a fun, original, casually morbid fantasy setting, and while Forget Me Not is certainly casually morbid, it feels neither original nor fun. It’s really not a game that I think is worth paying for. But, I couldn’t resist playing it for its clicker-like qualities despite this, so maybe I’m just a hypocrite.

There's the possibility it gets better later on with the addition of more plants and such, but the initial slog and piecemeal story does not offer incentive to get there. The clicking aspect has you just waiting most of the time rather than clicking rapidly like most clickers, which would be at least mildly stimulating. It would have actually been [i]better[/i] had the waiting process been longer, which would have allowed the game to be treated like an enjoyable virtual garden you can check in on every so often to see how its doing. This is the game that made me a fan of CAVYHOUSE, and ensured that any of their games that are on Steam will make their way to my library and be played to completion once I start them.

Forget Me Not is one of those types of doujin games that really need to be played to understand what the experience is like, since describing it as a "visual novel/clicker" really isn't doing justice to how the game feels to play. Yes, the clicker aspect is there, and it's satisfying if you like that kind of thing. And the story presented in the visual novel isn't particularly complex, but it does set up a certain charming but slightly creepy atmosphere that will be right in your wheelhouse if you enjoy miwashiba's games that are available on Steam (highly recommended, by the way). But these two elements, when put together with the striking artwork and soundtrack in this game, combine to become for a certainty more than the sum of parts implied by the descriptor "visual novel clicker".

So if you tend to enjoy off-beat or unique experiences, or you have enjoyed unusual doujin games in the past, I recommend checking out Forget Me Not. I will add that it is absolutely worthwhile to achieve the true ending, as the additional story context it provides made the conclusion wonderfully satisfying to me.

How can I describe Forget Me Not? It is one of those beautiful and bizarre Japanese games that defies genre, making it impossible to really explain to someone who hasn't played it. By definition you might call this an idle clicker, but there is no idle component, nor do you need an auto-clicker. You might call this a casual gardening game, but it has nothing in common with Farmville or anything like that.

In Forget Me Not, you tend an organ garden, though what the fruits are is purely a story device, and doesn't effect how you tend to them. You will spend your time clicking on frogs to keep your watering can filled, then clicking on your plants to keep them wet (shown as coloured). You click on fruit at various stages of growth to produce various qualities, which need to be submitted for jobs, which are bookended by nice little visual novel sections.

Forget Me Not is an incredibly relaxing game that truly allows you to no thoughts, empty mind while making constant progress, while retaining a slightly sinister aura to its story and your boss's interactions with her clients. Are you performing a service, or are you profiting from others' misery? This story of biological alchemy is truly one you need to experience for yourself.

You might mistakenly think that this is one of those cheap, achievement heavy games with no substance, but you'd be wrong. Forget Me Not makes you work for your progress, as simply as the work may be. There is always something to do and plants/animals to level up, so when you finally reach peak efficiency, you'll feel like you've earned every second of your crop yields; and make no mistake, finishing the game is not the end, as there are numerous post-game missions and plenty more to finish if you want to complete the achievement mural (finishing missions colours a tiny portion of a huge image).
This is one of the greatest clicker games I have had the pleasure of enjoying.

Ai-je aimé le jeu, l'ambiance, l'univers ? Oui.
Ai-je apprécié les personnages, le chara-design, l'histoire ? Oui.
Pour autant, recommanderais-je le jeu ? Non.

Pourquoi ? Parce que c'est du farming pur et simple. Plus d'une quinzaine d'heures (dans mon cas) passées à cliquer sur les mêmes objets, en boucle (pour obtenir la vraie fin). C'est un genre de gameplay que je ne recommande jamais et qui, de mon point de vue, n'apporte pas grand-chose puisqu'on en a très vite compris le principe. Sans compter qu'il n'y pas de système automatique comme dans Cookie Clicker qui permettent de laisser le jeu tourner tout seul : on devra passer chaque seconde la main scotchée à la souris et les yeux rivés sur l'écran.

Toutefois, personnellement, j'ai passé un bon moment, à découvrir les personnages, à m'immerger dans l'ambiance aigre-doux et un peu toquée du jeu. Donc si vous avez besoin de quelque chose pour vous vider le cerveau, ce jeu est parfait. Sinon, j'ai vu qu'il existait au moins une vidéo qui condensait toutes les cinématiques du jeu. Vous gagnerez un temps fou tout en découvrant cet univers décalé qui, je trouve, vaut le détour.
